newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. confirms Israel loan guarantees for 1997.
newsitem.headline: U.S. confirms Israel loan guarantees for 1997.

text.p: As the emergency Israeli-Arab summit continued in Washington on Wednesday, the U.S. confirmed further loan guarantees for Israel covering nearly $2 billion in the financial year starting October 1.
Israel's finance ministry said Washington will deduct only $60 million from the total of $2 billion loan guarantees previously agreed.
The deduction represents the amount Israel spent last year on Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, which the U.S. says are an obstacle to peace.

The Jerusalem Post newspaper said Israel had actually spent $307 million in the West Bank and Gaza in the last year but most of it went for construction of bypass roads which the U.S. does not take into account when making its deduction.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor said he was pleased that only $60 million would be deducted.

The announcement of the loan-guarantee total was made as President Bill Clinton was hosting an emergency Israeli-Arab summit in Washington in an attempt to get peace talks back on track following bloody clashes between Palestinians and Israelis that killed 72 people.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government, formed in June, has approved construction of thousands of new homes in Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza, lifting restrictions imposed by the previous Labour government.
Increased investment in settlements could mean that a greater sum would be deducted from the guarantees next year.
Last year the United States also deducted $60 million but in the previous year $217 million was deducted and in the year before that, the figure was $437 million.
The loan guarantees were approved in 1992 to help Israel absorb new immigrants, especially from the former Soviet Union.

Israel, the biggest single recipient of U.S. foreign aid, may raise a total of $10 billion with the backing of the guarantees until 1998, when the programme expires. So far it has raised about $6.6 billion.
After 1998 Israel will have to rely on its sovereign credit rating to raise funds on international markets.

In preparation, Israel has begun broadening its options. Last December it issued a $250 million Yankee bond, the first without a U.S. government guarantee. It now plans to raise $750 million in Europe over three years, including a debut Eurobond in November.

Last month Standard & Poor's and Moody's rating agencies reaffirmed Israel's A minus and A3 credit rating, respectively. This is equivalent to S&P's rating for Chile and just below those of the Czech Republic, Hong Kong, Iceland and Thailand.
Israel is also arranging its second syndicated bank loan abroad and next year plans to test the Asian market as well.
